summary: EarthTrend Explorer is a web app that lets anyone check whether the temperature or rainfall in an Indian state has really changed. We built it for the challenge Be An Earth System Detective.
details:
EarthTrend Explorer lets anyone check whether temperature or rainfall in an Indian state has really changed. The user picks one of 28 states, a variable (temperature or rainfall) and a range of years from 2003 to 2023. The app plots the yearly values with two trend lines and runs three tests: linear regression, the Kendall tau test and Sen's slope. It then gives a plain verdict: Increasing, Decreasing or No clear trend. A trend is reported only when regression and Kendall tau both give p < 0.05 and point in the same direction. A second page compares all 28 states at once using pre-calculated trends, showing which states changed most and how many results are significant.
Data from NASA
We used NASA POWER (T2M, air temperature at 2 m, in °C) and NASA Giovanni, which gave us the PRECTOTCORR variable (corrected precipitation, in mm/day). We turned them into yearly values for 28 states over 2003–2023, 1,176 yearly records in total.
Benefits
Students can learn to read real data and see what "statistically significant" means.
Journalists can fact-check claims such as "it's getting hotter here" for a specific state.
Local planners can see where change is real and where it is not.
No coding or data skills are needed, and the test results and units are shown, not just a chart.
Intended impact
We want more people to ask climate questions about their own region and answer them with evidence. Making NASA Earth data easy to check builds data literacy and helps tell real change from a few unusual years. Next steps are more NASA variables, district and city level, corrections for seasonality, regional languages and a mobile version.
Tools, languages and software
Python, pandas, NumPy, SciPy and Matplotlib for the analysis and charts, and Streamlit for the web app (we also made a Tkinter desktop version). Code is on GitHub. No special hardware was used, just ordinary laptops. We drafted code and slide content with AI assistance (Claude). No AI-generated images were used, and all screenshots come from our own app.
Creativity
It acts as a "detective": instead of only showing a chart, it gives a verdict a beginner can understand.
It says "no clear trend" when there isn't one, rather than forcing a story.
It requires two independent tests to agree, so one lucky result isn't enough.
Factors we considered
Honesty about limits: the p-values assume independent years, and the all-state page runs 56 tests (28 states × 2 variables), so about 3 are expected to look significant by chance. We treat results as leads to investigate, not proof of long-term climate change.
Clear units: every result is shown in °C or mm/day, and slopes are per year.
Data scope: the app's own notice says the values are not state-wide averages.
Beginner-friendliness: simple steps, plain wording and no jargon in the verdict.
Reliability: a fixed, repeatable rule for the verdict, so the same inputs always give the same answer.
